source.title: Polysemanticity and Capacity in Neural Networks

record.tranche_reason: The post summarizes a capacity-based account of polysemanticity in toy models, but does not test any of the listed claims about neuron-pole audit rates, modern language models, classic vision neurons, attribution graphs, or explanation scoring.
record.gate_note: The post reports its own toy-model findings about sparsity and polysemanticity; these are recorded under versions ["none"] because they do not measure a listed version. The cited observation from Elhage et al. is not recorded as a result of this study.
record.test_reason: This is a blog summary of a toy-model capacity-allocation paper. It reports no audit of neuron-pole jobs, no language or vision model neuron analysis, no attribution graphs and no explanation scoring. Its capacity-based account of polysemanticity runs against V4's 'not capacity' framing. But it is shown only in synthetic toy models and does not measure interpretable-neuron shares, so it does not test V4 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors frame polysemanticity as optimal capacity allocation under diminishing marginal returns, which they link to sparse features of similar importance. They are unsure of the work's importance and expect large models to be messier. The remark that architecture tweaks might change polysemanticity at a performance cost is a speculative comment by co-author Kshitij Sachan, not a result.
record.recipe_differences: The post summarizes a theoretical and numerical capacity-allocation analysis of toy models, not an audit of neuron explanations or activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported relationship varies with feature sparsity; the post says models showed qualitatively different levels of polysemanticity as sparsity changed.

fits_no_version.finding: In the toy model, the dense-feature regime (increasing marginal returns) shows no polysemanticity. The sparse regime (diminishing returns) shows polysemanticity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy models, polysemanticity arises as optimal capacity allocation when features are sparse and have diminishing marginal returns.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing sparsity increases polysemanticity across the authors' toy models, with qualitatively different levels between models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy models, polysemanticity rises with feature sparsity, and its level depends on the model.

record.problems: The post does not name the models behind its aggregate sparsity statement or give numerical results, uncertainty estimates, or controls. It notes that the large-model story may be substantially messier.
record.rows_left_out: The post also mentions a block-semi-orthogonal structure with differing block sizes, but this does not measure neuron interpretability or polysemanticity rates named in the claim. The observation attributed to Elhage et al. is cited rather than a result of this study.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or shares.
No other language models, dense/MoE comparison, or scale.
No measurement of interpretable-neuron share versus architecture, regularization or tools. The capacity argument is toy-model theory only.
No attribution graphs or reconstruction error.
No test of explanations beyond activating examples.

record.verdict_notes: The post's capacity-based view is conceptually opposed to V4 and to the 'already clean' essay. It offers no evidence on real-model neuron interpretability rates, so no verdict is given. The block-semi-orthogonal structure finding is correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or neuron-pole job counts.
No comparable language-model audits, dense/MoE comparison, or model-scale sweep.
No analysis of InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron or recursive generalization.
No test of architecture, regularization, interpretability tools, or the stated Inception-sized model estimates.
No test of explanations against activations beyond the examples used to write them.
No automated scoring of neuron explanations on new text.
